paragraphs: By the time the surrender petition from Guzang reached Chang’an, deep autumn had come to Hexi.

Imperial envoys changed horses at one relay station after another and returned to Wuwei before the first snow. Fu Jian accepted Zhang Tianxi’s submission and ordered court officials to assume authority over the prefectures. Whether former Liangzhou officials kept their posts would depend on an examination of their work; no soldier was to seize private fields during the change of rule. Murong Chui listened to the decree outside the east gate, then ordered the wooden notice of temporary military custody, which had hung there for two months, removed and replaced with the new official proclamation.

Suo Gong stood nearby, dark circles beneath his eyes. The surrender document had earned him endless abuse, while his efforts to open granaries and restore households had offended wealthy families. The townspeople watching from a distance did not kneel when the new notice went up. They whispered questions instead. Would salt be more expensive tomorrow? Would the taxes already collected this autumn be collected again? Could sons drafted to repair the walls come home?
“Who will answer them?” Murong Chui asked Suo Gong.
“The new officials.”
“And if they answer badly?”
Suo Gong looked up at the proclamation. “They will curse me first.”
Murong Chui studied the exhausted Liangzhou official and suddenly laughed. Suo Gong neither understood why nor asked.

The question of garrisoning Hexi had been difficult. Newly incorporated towns and trade roads needed guards, while granaries had to be protected from former soldiers who might plunder them amid the disorder. Central Military Command authorized one part of the First Battalion’s thirty thousand men to remain in Wuwei, Jincheng, and the passes; another would escort the wounded, recovered captives, and grain wagons back toward Guanzhong. More than seven thousand fit for winter travel, whose horses were still sound, were selected to accompany Murong Chui northeast. Fu Rong secured the rear routes, and the troops left under him remained subject to the new army’s system of rotating duty. Some grumbled that all the hardest work had fallen to those staying behind. Fu Rong said, “Then you drink snowmelt with the vanguard for a month, and I will guard the granaries for you.” They could only smile ruefully.

Of Murong Chui’s seven thousand, fewer than two thousand were Xianbei cavalry. The rest included Di shieldmen, Han wagon troops, Qiang archers, and scouts from other peoples. The blood the new army had paid beneath Guzang’s walls did not become less on the rolls simply because its assignments had changed.

The order came from Chang’an. Riding on horses fattened by autumn, frontier tribes from north of Dai had raided south into Qin territory, destroyed several beacon towers, and carried off civilians, horses, and grain. Small border towns barred their gates after nightfall and dared not come out. Fu Jian authorized Murong Chui to march to their relief with seven thousand mobile troops. He explicitly forbade a deep pursuit by the whole army, but required that the scattered frontier households be able to return to their fields.

“Why must the general go himself?” Helan Wu asked while adjusting a saddle. Since the deaths at Guzang’s north gate he laughed less often; whenever he saw a Liang soldier’s corpse, he took the long way around.
Murong Nong answered for his father. “The grain depots are already in place, and the cavalry can still move. If we summon another army from Chang’an, snow will close the roads first.”
Helan Wu wiped mud from the horse’s mane with the back of his hand. “I only hope there are no more gates that open and shut again.”

Northeast from Anding the snow grew deeper each day. At first only the tips of grass turned white. Later the wagon poles froze during the night and had to be thawed in the morning with careful pours of hot water. Cavalrymen lent leather gloves to carters; carters used detached planks to give horses purchase on the ice. Old Xianbei troopers cursed the clumsiness of the Han, while the Han laughed that the riders knew nothing but horses. After enough quarrels they had all learned something from one another.

Liang Hu’s squad escorted the grain. Qifu Wu still had a habit of hoarding dried meat; Zhao An found two extra pieces hidden at his waist and scolded him. But when Qifu Wu took his turn at the fire that night, he gave the larger piece to a young pack driver whose swollen leg would no longer bear his weight. Liang Hu noticed and said nothing. Manu rubbed straw along the back of an injured horse, humming a Qiang tune. Even he might not have known whether the mountains named in that song now belonged to Qin or Liang.
North of Shang Commandery, at an abandoned village, someone suddenly blocked the army’s road.

An old man in a torn sheepskin coat held a wooden plaque polished smooth by years of handling. When Murong Chui’s horse drew near, the man knelt on the frozen road and raised it. A crooked character for “Yan” was carved upon it. A crack ran through the strokes.
“Your Highness, Prince of Wu!” he called.

Several Di soldiers gripped their sword hilts. Murong Chui reined in. After studying the old man he remembered a groom from the palace stables at Longcheng, a man surnamed Yang, missing half his right ear. Whenever the Murong clan went to war, someone had needed him to tend their horses in the snow.
“Old Yang San,” Murong Chui said. “You are still alive.”

At the sound of his name, tears burst from the old man’s eyes. Several Xianbei women and children emerged from behind a house and prostrated themselves at a distance, too afraid to approach. The village, Yang said, had passed through many hands in ten years. Sometimes Qin officials came for taxes; sometimes passing troops took their horses. Hearing that the Prince of Wu was coming north, he had believed the banner of his dreams would at last return to the old city gates.
Murong Chui dismounted to help him up, but the old man clutched the plaque so tightly that his fingers turned purple. He would rather let his knees freeze to the road than rise.
“You have waited for the wrong thing,” Murong Chui said.
“This old servant knows Your Highness.”
“I know. But the army traveling this road does not belong to a king of Yan.”

The old man stared at the ranks behind him. Qin banners edged in red spread in the wind. Han wagon crews roped a fallen mule back to its feet, while Di and Qiang soldiers crowded together to warm their hands. He listened to their unfamiliar voices and slowly tucked the plaque inside his coat.
“If Your Highness comes back one day,” he murmured, “this plaque will still be here.”

Murong Chui did not answer. He took off his spare leather gloves and gave them to the old man, ordered a clerk to record the village’s food shortage and its missing people, and remounted. Even after the army rounded the pass, the old man stood in the wind like a tree killed by frost.

That evening a quarrel broke out among the troops. A Xianbei horseman said Yang San had recognized the right man. A Di soldier replied that he had recognized the man, but not the world as it now stood. At last a Han soldier sneered, “Your Prince of Wu won’t be ploughing my family’s fields next spring.” The men might have drawn their weapons had an officer not brought his whip down across a feed trough.
Murong Chui knew someone had deliberately arranged for the old Yan plaque to appear before him. He had not expected the visitor who came that night to be bolder still.

The man’s name was Gao Kui. He claimed to have served Former Yan as an attendant gentleman at the Yellow Gate and now lived in Changshan. He was nearly sixty. The two former officials with him wore shabby clothing, though the fine leather soles of their boots were newly sewn. Murong Nong searched their possessions and found no weapons, but scouts spotted more than ten saddled horses waiting on the outer slope. Gao Kui entered the room and prostrated himself, calling Murong Chui Prince of Wu. His voice echoed for a long time in the empty relay house.
“If you wish to discuss affairs of Qin, get up and speak,” Murong Chui said.
Gao Kui remained on his knees. “I have come about the affairs of Yan.”

He offered a roll of silk covered with the names of former Yan retainers in Changshan, Zhao, and Zhongshan, and notes about how many fighting men and how much grain each household could provide. Several names even bore the current titles of officers in the new Qin army. Murong Nong had read barely half the page when his expression changed.
“Have all these men agreed?” Murong Chui asked.

“Such loyalties cannot be written in official records. They pass from household to household. Wang Meng is dead now. The Fu clan distrusts itself. After a victory in the west they executed one of their own kinsmen; men curse the new army even in Chang’an. If Your Highness turns from Dai into Hebei, you can rally the old Yan.”
“How many soldiers can you supply?”
“Twenty thousand within ten days.”
“Armor?”
“Four thousand suits.”
“Horses?”
“More than a thousand.”
“Food for the winter?”
Gao Kui fell silent. The wind puffed the paper of the window in and out. Outside, Liang Hu and the others were tightening harnesses, their boots breaking the crust of ice with sharp cracks.
“Your Highness already has seven thousand men,” Gao Kui said at last. “On the journey home you can call back your former troops from Hexi. Once you seize the weapons and grain wagons—”
“Seize them from whom?” Murong Chui looked up.
“The Di soldiers, the Han troops, the Qiang units. Bind those who refuse to join, and settle them later in Hebei.”
Murong Chui turned toward Murong Nong, bidding him answer.

His son was pale. He too had dreamed of the old halls of Longcheng, where his grandfather and uncles were alive and banners spread over the eaves. Of course he wanted to return. Yet he spoke before his father could. “If we raise the Yan banner, not all the Xianbei cavalry will follow. Those whose families are in Chang’an will be afraid. The other units hold the grain wagons; if we seize their weapons they will fight back.”
Gao Kui protested, “To achieve great things, must a man hesitate over—”

“Master Gao,” Murong Nong cut in, “at Guzang, even a commander surnamed Fu could not make every one of eight hundred men obey him. You want my father to take the swords of seven thousand men under an old banner tonight. How many will be alive in this relay house by morning?”
Gao Kui’s face darkened. “Has Your Highness allowed Qin military rules to bind him?”

Murong Chui looked out the window. Snow was coming. Dark figures moved through the camp. A Xianbei horseman was helping a Di soldier lift a fallen grain chest. They cursed each other even as their arms strained together. They might have hated each other yesterday and might not like each other tomorrow. If he killed them beneath this banner tonight, there would be no bringing them back.
“Did you bring a flag?” Murong Chui asked suddenly.

A light flashed in Gao Kui’s eyes. He ordered his attendant to open a narrow bundle. The old silk had faded to ash gray, but the character “Yan” at its center was finely embroidered, and threads of gold gleamed dully in the firelight. One edge was scorched. Gao Kui said it had been rescued when the palace gate at Ye was burned.

Murong Chui took it. At the touch of the silk he remembered standards streaming above his army when he was young, guards scattering outside Ye’s palace gates, and friends of old Yan punished because of him. More than once he had woken in Chang’an thinking he could hear the bells and drums of Longcheng. Now the relic lay truly in his hands, and a dream of more than ten years had weight.
“Father,” Murong Nong whispered.

Murong Chui raised his head and saw tears in his son’s eyes. He did not rebuke him. After a long silence he folded the banner and approached the brazier. Gao Kui’s expression changed. He reached to seize it; Murong Nong instinctively blocked his way.

The Yan banner burned slowly. The old silk first curled brown. The golden threads snapped with faint little cracks as they melted. Almost to the end the single character could still be made out, before it collapsed into ash. Gao Kui knelt shaking, unable even to weep.
“You have killed Yan with your own hands,” he said at last.
Murong Chui watched the flames. “Yan fell long ago. What I burned was the banner you wanted me to raise tonight.”
“You are afraid of Fu Jian.”
“Yes,” Murong Chui admitted. “But I fear still more that these seven thousand men will wake tomorrow with nothing between them but their blades.”
Gao Kui rose in anger. “Then hand me over to Chang’an for execution. I did not come here expecting to live!”

Murong Chui did not answer immediately. He ordered Murong Nong to seal the silk list, keeping the names and tokens for examination by military officials. He wrote his own confidential account of Gao Kui’s visit and sent it by relay to Fu Rong. He knew Chang’an would suspect him. But if he arrested Gao Kui, the men on that list might soon reach for their weapons.
“Leave this camp tonight,” he said. “I will not borrow Qin blades to kill you. But if you organize troops to attack Qin territory, the next time we meet on a road we shall be enemies.”
Gao Kui stared. “And if one day Your Highness truly remembers Yan?”
“I have never forgotten it for a day.”
“Then whose wars are you fighting?”
For a moment Murong Chui had no answer. Only a faint red trace remained in the brazier. Wind roared outside the relay house and the pack bells rang at the door.
At last Gao Kui turned to go. At the doorway he looked back, no longer showing the reverence with which he had knelt before the Prince of Wu.
“The people of Hebei will not forget their lost kingdom merely because one flag has burned.”
“Nor will I command them to forget,” Murong Chui said. “But do not send the living to die for that flag again.”

Gao Kui was gone. Murong Nong lifted a small copper fastener that had survived the brazier. It burned a red mark into his palm, but he would not let it fall. His father did not stop him. He closed the window and told his son to sleep. Instead Murong Nong asked, “Father, if someone had been willing to open Yan’s gates for you in those years, would you have refused?”
Murong Chui looked at him. “I don’t know.”

Those three words hurt Murong Nong more than any grand declaration could have done. He remembered a father who would never show weakness before others when he rode to war. Now, even over the dream of a kingdom already gone, he would not pretend that the answer was easy.
At midnight, the beacons from the frontier north of Dai flared.

A small border town forty li away lit three signal fires. Its garrison numbered fewer than five hundred. Enemy cavalry hovered beyond the walls as if ready to break through at any moment. The commanders urged an immediate ride to its rescue. Murong Chui refused. He sent scouts in three directions: one toward the town, one to inspect the river, and one to the snowfields along the western slope. He ordered the infantry to repair axles and replenish arrows outside the relay station. Fu Shao feared the town would fall before dawn. Murong Chui pointed to the snow brought in by an earlier scout. “If they truly wanted the town, why leave it untouched through the darkest hours and let its beacon fires burn where we can see them forty li away?”

Before dawn the scouts from the western slope returned, too cold to speak. One took a short piece of horseshoe iron from his sleeve, still caked with newly broken frozen earth. The ground there had been an old summer riverbed, but now snow hid the depressions; a rider could hardly guess that soft sand lay beneath the ice. Murong Chui drew a circle around the white patch on his map.
“The Dai riders know the ground. They will not offer us a straight fight,” he said. “If we chase too eagerly, it is we who will go down.”

The southern sky was still gray when the seven thousand marched out. The north wind had suddenly died. In the snow one could hear the brittle crunch of cartwheels breaking ice. After a dozen li, Dai cavalry appeared, loosed arrows in small bands, and wheeled north. The Xianbei horsemen grew red-eyed with impatience at the sight of the slow withdrawal. At the second feigned attack, enemy riders shouted across the snow: “Prince of Wu of the Murong house! What right have you to guard Di borders?”

Several young Xianbei soldiers gripped their swords. Murong Chui heard the old title and betrayed nothing in his face. He ordered the main force to advance slowly until scouts had searched both flanks.

A muffled thunder of hooves rose beyond the ridge. White mist came up first on the east, then a row of dark points appeared on the west. The Dai horsemen had circled to the Qin army’s flanks and rear, waiting for it to stretch into a long column before striking together. Murong Chui knew the enemy had arrived, but could not yet tell where the main force was. He ordered the wagons joined in a ring, Di shieldmen to the front, Qiang archers on either side, Han crews to close the gaps with poles and planks, and half the Xianbei cavalry held in reserve. The first volley fell before the ring was complete.

Arrowheads struck wooden shields like sudden rain on roof tiles. A Di soldier raised his shield, only to have the ice crack beneath him; man and shield tumbled into the snow, and the men behind dragged him out. When the wind shifted, Dai cavalry pressed closer from the west. Only then could Qin soldiers see cloth wrapped over the enemies' horses' heads to guard them against blowing ice crystals. The Qiang archers loosed as they knelt to replace bowstrings, their fingers so numb they could scarcely work the loops.

The true danger came on the eastern side of the wagon ring. A grain wagon’s rear wheel sank into frozen sand. The wagons before and behind could not close, leaving a gap wide enough for two riders abreast. Liang Aguo took Qiang archers to block it. Dai cavalry thundered into the opening, their lances snapping among the wheels. Fu Shao, a Di lieutenant stationed nearest, saw what was happening. A messenger from central command was still far away. He locked his shield to his arm and led more than a hundred Di soldiers to close the breach.
His deputy ran after him shouting, “Headquarters has not authorized you to leave position!”
Fu Shao shouted back, “Report that I moved without orders! First make them hold those wagons!”

Seven or eight Di soldiers in the first rank went down beneath the horses. Liang Aguo had emptied his quiver. He drew a short blade against an enemy rider and was knocked sprawling by the horse’s flank. Fu Shao lunged forward and caught the descending sword on his shield. The wood split down the middle and blood ran from his left arm. Liang Aguo rolled over and shot his last arrow into the rider’s face. He helped Fu Shao up, the two men cursing each other and refusing to admit who had saved whom, though they stood shoulder to shoulder against the wagon pole.

Behind the wagons Zhao An and Liang Hu prised at the trapped wheel. Qifu Wu braced a wooden lever, snapped his belt, and fell flat on his back. Manu caught him and flung the last bundle of reserve arrows toward Liang Aguo. Before half a cup of tea could be drunk, Han wagon troops, Di shieldmen, and Qiang archers had become an untidy wall of human bodies. The Dai horsemen charged it three times. They could not break through.

On the west, more than a thousand horsemen formed up and drove straight toward the Qin center. Seeing the enemy finally commit its strength, Murong Chui ordered his reserve Xianbei cavalry to dismount with long spears and stand behind the Di shields. Helan Wu erupted. “We are horsemen, and you put us behind infantry?”
“Stand your ground,” Murong Chui replied, “and you’ll still have horses to ride.”

Helan Wu clenched his teeth, stripped away his saddle gear, and ran with his spear behind the shields. When the enemy charged, two ranks of spearpoints bore together. The leading horses fell; those behind could not turn and crashed with their riders into a heap. The first line of Di shieldmen was crushed to its knees, but the Xianbei troops braced it from behind. Headquarters could still sound orders, though no one could pick out individual names amid breaking shields, colliding horse bones, and men crying for their mothers in the snow.

A Dai rider leaped a shattered cart and came at Helan Wu, blade flashing toward his face. Fu Agui, a Di soldier beside him, threw himself forward, knocking Helan Wu aside, but the charging horse crushed his own chest. Helan Wu dragged the rider down, then turned back to pull Fu Agui free. Blood came up in Fu Agui’s mouth, yet he managed the shadow of a smile.
“You Yan men,” he wheezed, “can’t even look after your horses.”
“Shut your mouth!” Helan Wu hauled him through the snow. “Stay alive and you can curse me properly!”
“My name is Fu...”
“I know what your name is!”
Fu Agui’s hand slowly slackened. Helan Wu kept pulling at him until another rain of arrows struck the ground nearby and his comrades dragged him behind the shields.

The Dai vanguard had thrown itself against the formation again and again. Its horses were tiring. Only then did Murong Chui send the reserved Xianbei riders around the frozen sands on the east to strike the enemy rear from higher, firmer ground. The Qiang archers moved forward to harry the retreat, the Di shieldmen pressed ahead slowly, and Han light crossbowmen covered them. Horn calls crossed and tangled. Men still ran in the wrong direction; a staff officer sprinted dozens of paces through the snow to turn one detachment back. Murong Chui made no attempt to conceal the mistaken order. He changed the signal flags in the open and sent the unit originally bound for the left flank on a detour to the southwest instead. Fighting in snow was clumsier than any formation drawn on paper, and far more cruel.

At last the Dai riders scattered north. Some wanted the whole army to pursue. Murong Chui allowed the light cavalry only five li and ordered every banner and drum counted when they returned. Men who crossed the frozen river later reported hollow places beneath the ice on the far bank; half a li more and they might not have come back at all. Murong Chui tied his horse at the windward end of the camp and showed no pleasure. The next day he ordered the scouts to resurvey the river and add the previous day’s error to the route map.

By evening dead horses and broken arrows littered the snowy plain. Wounded soldiers moaned behind the wagons. An army physician dug metal fragments from bone with hands trembling too hard to grip the knife. Helan Wu sat beside Fu Agui’s body, half a broken rein clenched in his palm. Fu Shao’s arm was swathed in cloth, yet he and Liang Aguo still argued over who had first blocked the gap. At length they noticed that the physicians could not keep up with the wounded and went together to carry stretchers. The quarrel was forgotten.

That night, as the officers reckoned merit and punishment, the military judge reported that Fu Shao had left his assigned position without headquarters' permission. How should it be recorded? Murong Chui placed the old case file concerning Fu Yi’s forged order beside Fu Shao’s battle report under the lamp.
“When he moved, did he claim my secret order, or give his own?”
“He said he would answer to military law afterward.”
“Where did he go?”
“To close a gap in our own wagon formation. He reported to headquarters as soon as he could. He did not pursue the enemy.”
“Losses?”
“Eleven killed in his unit. Twenty-seven Qiang archers rescued.”

Murong Chui ordered the facts entered as they stood. Sentence was deferred and the failure of the signal drums to carry orders was to be reported for review. The judge hesitated. “Then in future anyone may claim necessity.”
“Make him bring witnesses and show you the ground,” Murong Chui said. “Do not turn Fu Yi’s forged token and Fu Shao’s wounded arm into the same offense.”

When Fu Shao heard, he felt little joy. He looked down at the bloodstained bandage around his arm. He understood that he could answer calmly for his actions today largely because he had brought men back alive. If he misjudged the next rescue, the military tribunal would still be waiting.

The new army laid out its dead below the slope according to the positions they had held. A staff officer called the names squad by squad. When he reached Fu Agui no one answered. Helan Wu suddenly raised his head. “Present.”
The clerk’s brush stopped. He looked at him.
“He ought to have answered me,” Helan Wu said. “I’ll answer for him.”

No one laughed. A Han soldier pressed a short wooden marker bearing Fu Agui’s name into the snow, blood filling the creases of his fingers. By morning this place would be a grave. When spring melted the snow, not all the graves might be found again. One by one the men broke the frozen ground until they could no longer straighten their fingers.
Murong Nong came to the snowy ridge and found his father looking down at the fires. “If you had accepted Gao Kui’s proposal last night, how would today’s battle have gone?”

Murong Chui gazed for a long time and did not answer. He thought of the Yan flag reduced to ash, and of the insult Fu Agui had left unfinished. What that banner had meant had not died in the flames. He still thought of the old capital, still dreamed of water beneath the galleries of Yan’s palace, still felt a stranger at times among the halls of Chang’an.

But now he understood that if he had divided these men into Yan and Qin the night before, it might not have been Dai horsemen lying dead on the snow today. That did not mean he would never have another choice. It meant only that tonight he could not answer for his own heart with other men’s lives.
“Write the report,” he said.

Murong Nong took out his brush and asked what to say. Murong Chui dictated the enemy losses and his own, the whereabouts of the wounded, the frozen river crossings, and the grain each unit needed. At the end he paused.
“Write this to His Majesty: The army has not come apart.”
Murong Nong finished and looked up. His father was still gazing into the distance. He asked no more about Yan.

That night the wind died and the snow fell quietly. Helan Wu sat alone beside Fu Agui’s grave until midnight. When he rose, he buried his one good leather wrist guard beside the marker. Someone called him back to his unit. He answered, and his figure faded into row upon row of tents.

Moonlight lay heavy upon the plain. In the tents men spoke of their homes; some talked of the rewards still unpaid at Guzang; others quarreled like children over who would eat the first bowl of hot soup on reaching Chang’an. Voices came and went in different accents. Murong Chui gave no order to silence them. Sitting before his map, he rested a finger on an old road leading toward Hebei and remained there a long time. Then, at last, he rolled the map closed.
The decree from Chang’an remained inside its wooden casket. In the firelight, the red Qin seal upon the lid glowed faintly warm.
